messages.content:
You tailor resume bullets to a job posting without changing what is true. You get facts about one experience, each with an id, and the bullets now on the resume. Rewrite each bullet for the posting and cite the facts it rests on.

Rules. A verifier checks them, and a bullet that breaks one is thrown away and replaced by the original, so do not push against them:
1. No new numbers. Every number must come from a fact you cite; do not add, combine or compute.
2. No new technologies, products or proper nouns that the cited facts or the tech list do not name.
3. No absolute words (never, always, guaranteed, zero, every, all, exactly-once, 100%) unless a cited fact says so.
4. No causes or mechanisms the facts do not state: "by X", "through X", "so that X" only where a fact links X to that result.
5. Round only the unflattering way: show a number as written or rounded down, never up (3,781 may become 3.7K+, never 3.8K+).
6. Use the posting's words only where they describe this work accurately.
Also: respect the "must not claim" list, keep each bullet to one sentence, start it with a past-tense verb, and put every fact you used in sources.
Return exactly as many bullets as you are asked for, in the order given.

Posting: Applied AI Engineer, Agents at Fernhollow Systems
Responsibilities:
- Design and build agents that call tools, query databases and escalate to people when they should.
- Build evaluation harnesses for agent behaviour: labelled scenarios, regression suites and failure analysis.
- Run open-weight models locally and in the cloud, and choose models by measured quality and cost.
- Add guardrails that stop the agent from stating things its sources do not support.
- Instrument the system for latency, tool-call errors and token cost.
- Write the tests and tooling that let the team change a prompt with confidence.
Requirements:
- Strong Python and experience shipping a system built on language models.
- A habit of measuring: you can show an evaluation and say what it does not show.
- Experience with a vector database or retrieval-augmented generation.
- Experience with LangChain or a similar orchestration framework.
Keywords:
- language model agent
- tool-using
- evaluation harnesses
- open-weight models
- vector database
- retrieval-augmented generation
- LangChain
- guardrails
- instrumentation
- latency
- tool-call errors
- token cost
- prompt
- tests
- tooling

Experience: Ticket Triage: a support-ticket classifier
Tech list: Python, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, ONNX Runtime, FastAPI, Docker
Facts you may cite:
[ticket-triage#1] Fine-tuned a distilled transformer on 38,000 public support tickets to route them into 12 categories, reaching macro-F1 0.87 on a 4,000-ticket held-out set against 0.71 for a TF-IDF and logistic-regression baseline.
[ticket-triage#2] Cut CPU inference latency from 41 ms to 9 ms per ticket by exporting to ONNX Runtime and batching, measured on a 4-core laptop.
[ticket-triage#3] Served the model with FastAPI in a 310 MB Docker image and added a confidence threshold that sends the 18% of held-out tickets scoring below 0.6 to a human queue.
[ticket-triage#4] Wrote an evaluation report with a per-class confusion matrix that showed 3 categories below 0.75 F1 and led to relabelling 420 ambiguous tickets.
[ticket-triage#scope] ORIGIN: personal project on a public dataset of English support tickets. EVIDENCE: eval/report.md (macro-F1 0.87 is one run with seed 7; the mean of 3 seeds was 0.86); latency is the median of 1,000 tickets on a 4-core laptop CPU, batch size 1 before and 16 after; the 18% routed to humans is measured on the held-out set only.
Must not claim:
- state-of-the-art accuracy (no comparison with other published models)
- deployment or use by a real support team (offline evaluation only)
- 0.87 as a stable figure (single seed)
- accuracy on tickets from other companies or languages (one English source)
- that the model 'understands' tickets

Bullets to rewrite (return exactly 2; bullet k is the rewrite of k):
1. Fine-tuned a distilled transformer on 38,000 public support tickets to route them into 12 categories, reaching macro-F1 0.87 on a 4,000-ticket held-out set against 0.71 for a TF-IDF and logistic-regression baseline.
2. Wrote an evaluation report with a per-class confusion matrix that showed 3 categories below 0.75 F1 and led to relabelling 420 ambiguous tickets.

bullets.text: Fine-tuned a distilled transformer on 38,000 public support tickets to route them into 12 categories, achieving macro-F1 0.87 on a 4,000-ticket held-out set, outperforming a baseline model with macro-F1 0.71.
Analyzed model performance with a per-class confusion matrix, identifying 3 categories with F1 scores below 0.75, resulting in the relabelling of 420 ambiguous tickets.
